transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose it’s not anything terribly dramatic, but I’ve noticed I’m sort of… always on the go, even when there’s no real reason to be. Like on a quiet day, I’ll start with my garden club list, then suddenly I’m in my knitting bag, and then I’m looking at travel papers, and I haven’t really finished the first thing.  

I don’t know if that’s the sort of thing you mean, but it feels like I’m always up and moving from one thing to the next.
Is this feeling of being constantly on the go and jumping between tasks something new that started recently, or has it been a pattern for you since childhood or early adulthood?

Oh, I don’t think it’s new, no. I mean, I managed all right, so I don’t want to make it sound worse than it was… but even in grade school my teachers would tell my mother I was bright, just sort of scattered.  

They’d say I was always losing papers, talking before I was supposed to, and wiggling around in my seat before I’d finished my work. So yes, I suppose it has been there a long time, if that’s helpful.

latest_inference.note: The lifelong childhood-onset pattern of distractibility, impulsivity (talking out of turn), and hyperactivity (fidgeting, losing papers) reported since grade school is classic for ADHD and not consistent with episodic mood disorders (F30.x, F31.x), anxiety (F41.1), or personality pathology (F60.3), which are ruled out.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient describes lifelong, pervasive pattern beginning in early childhood (documented by teachers before age 12) characterized by inattention (losing items, difficulty completing tasks, jumping between activities) and hyperactive-impulsive traits (fidgeting, talking out of turn, restlessness). Symptoms are chronic, trait-like, and consistent with combined presentation of ADHD rather than an acute mood or anxiety disorder. No episodic mood elevation, psychosis, or discrete depressive/manic episodes reported, ruling out bipolar or other mood disorders. Presentation aligns with predominantly inattentive-hyperactive subtype meeting criteria for ADHD, combined type.
